To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IL-6 production is decreased in SLE patients, that the ratio of soluble IL-6 receptors to anti-IL 6 in SLE patients' plasma is skewed, and that the ratio of the soluble receptors to the anti-IL- 6 is directly proportional to IL-6 production by SLE patients' cells in vitro.

the plasma levels of anti-IL6 in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are elevated compared to healthy controls and that this elevation correlates with the production of IL-6 by the patient's peripheral blood mononucleocytes (PBMC).
IL-6 is not increased in SLE patients, but the ratio of soluble IL-6 receptors to anti-IL6 is increased.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of anti-interleukin- 6 (IL-6) and soluble IL-6 receptors (sIL-6R) with IL-6 and their potential contribution to the homeostatic regulation of IL-6 in vivo.
the interaction of soluble receptors and anti-cytokines in the regulation of cytokines in systemic lupus erythematosus.
the role of IL-6 in the pathogenesis of lupus and the role of anti-IL6 and soluble IL-6R in modulating IL-6 function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-6 is not involved in the pathogenesis of SLE.
the lupus patients' peripheral blood mononucleated cells are producing less IL-6 than normal cells and that the plasma of lupus patients has the capacity to block IL-6 activity.
the IL-6 system is involved in the disease process of SLE and the anti-IL- 6 system may be a mechanism to down regulate the IL-6 response in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lupus patients have an increased capacity to produce IL-6 and that the increased IL-6 is bound by soluble receptors and anti-IL- 6.
lupus patients have an increased soluble receptor/anti-interleukin- 6 ratio which may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.
lupus cells produce less IL-6 in vivo and in vitro than normal cells, and that this may be due in part to the presence of anti-IL6.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the anti-interleukin- 6 activity of lupus plasma is due to the presence of anti-interleukins in the plasma and that these anti-interleukines compete for the binding of interleukins to their receptors.

the interaction of anti-interleukin- 6 and interleukin-6 receptor with interleukin- 5 may contribute to the homoeostasis in interleukin-5 activity in vivo and that skewing of the interleukin- receptor/anti-interleukin ratio may contribute to the systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) disease process.
the interaction of anti-interleukin- 6 (IL-6) with IL-6 and IL 6 receptor may be important in regulating IL-6 activity and that this interaction may be altered in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
